summary: Discovery call to understand Ventura Financial's reliability and incident-tolerance requirements for LLM-powered features. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private, multi-region routing, automatic fallbacks to model variants and regions, KV/prefix cache implications across regions, expected RTO/RPO, and security/compliance needs. Agreed next steps: share security pack, benchmark sheet, and schedule SE deep dive.
topics: KV cache and prefix caching across regions
transcript: Meeting header: Recorded at 2026-04-05T16:00:00Z, Duration 47m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Ventura Head of Platform), Ravi Shah (Ventura SRE), Nicole Park (Ventura Security), Tom Nguyen (PM)
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros?

[00:12] Lena (Ventura): Hi, Lena here, head of platform at Ventura Financial. We're looking at adding LLM features to customer support flows and high-value transactions — must be low latency and extremely reliable.

[00:28] Maya: Great, and Ethan from our SE team will cover technical bits. Quick call agenda: understand your reliability needs, discuss hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, and cover fallback and multi-region options.
[00:45] Ethan (Redwood SE): Hey all, quick context questions: what's your current traffic profile and tolerance for partial outages? Is there a regulatory constraint on data residency?

[01:05] Ravi (Ventura SRE): We average ~2k qps at peak for chat-like requests, bursts to 4k during promos. We have a 99.95% availability SLO on the user-facing API and a 500ms P90 latency target for simple prompts. Data residency: EU for EU customers, US for NA — some cross-region calls ok but PII must be limited and encrypted.
[01:36] Nicole (Security): We need SOC2, audit logs, KMS integration, and the ability to keep keys in our HSM for private deployments. Also SSO/SAML and RBAC for ops.

[01:52] Maya: Totally. Those are common asks. Quick note: Redwood Hosted supports region pinning and per-request region hints; Dedicated/Private give you stronger isolation and allow customer-managed KMS.
[02:10] Tom (PM): What's the primary tradeoff between Hosted vs Dedicated from a reliability perspective?

[02:17] Ethan: Good question. Hosted is easiest to get started with and we operate multi-region failover for many customers. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and more predictable throughput under load — it also lowers the blast radius because it's isolated. Private gives you the most control for compliance but you manage more of the ops.
[02:40] Lena: For failover, do you support automatic routing between regions? We need sub-30s failover for region-level outages.

[02:48] Ethan: Yes, Redwood supports configurable routing policies. You can set primary region with automatic failover to a secondary region. Typical detection is based on health checks and error budgets; failover can be quick, but warm caches matter — if you failover cold you can see latency spikes while KV and prefix caches repopulate.
[03:12] Ravi: That's my worry — our models rely on prefix caching and key-value cache to keep latency low. How do you handle KV cache consistency across regions?

[03:22] Ethan: Right, KV cache isn't instantly replicated by default. Our runtime offers two approaches: soft-fallback where the secondary region can serve with a cold cache (higher latency but still functional), or active replication where we replicate cache state across regions at some cost and complexity. For most customers we recommend a hybrid: critical prefixes replicated, less frequent ones fetched on demand.
[03:52] Lena: Active replication — any ballpark for the added latency/cost?

[03:58] Ethan: It depends on throughput and TTLs; rough rule-of-thumb is 10-25% added token cost for continuous replication patterns, and you'd need to accept slightly higher inter-region egress. We'll send a benchmark sheet with a modeled run for your 2k qps profile.
[04:15] Nicole: From a security angle, does active replication move PII out of region? We need to ensure encryption in transit and at rest and that keys are customer-managed.

[04:26] Maya: For Hosted we can encrypt in transit and at rest and offer KMS integrations; customer-managed keys are available on Dedicated and Private. For Hosted we support Bring-Your-Own-Key via cloud KMS in many regions, but if you require on-prem HSM we recommend Private deployment.
[04:45] Ravi: SLA expectations — if we put a 99.95% target on the LLM endpoint, what can Redwood guarantee?

[04:52] Ethan: For Redwood Hosted we publish best-effort SLOs; Dedicated comes with contract-backed SLAs with uptime and latency targets depending on committed capacity. Private is negotiated. For your SLO 99.95%, Dedicated would be the recommended path, with multi-node pools and cross-AZ redundancy.
[05:15] Lena: How do fallbacks work at the model level? Can you fallback to cheaper models or local cached responses during incidents?

[05:23] Ethan: Yes. Our routing layer can fallback along several axes: model variant (smaller quantized model), capacity tier (dedicated -> hosted spot), and region. We also support cached response fallback for deterministic prompts — prefix caching or saved canned responses. You define policies: e.g., if P50 latency > 800ms or error rate > 1%, route to smaller model in the same region or to secondary region.
[05:55] Tom: Is switching models seamless — do you lose session context and KV cache?

[06:02] Ethan: Switching models can lose model-specific KV state; we try to preserve prompt-level context but embeddings and caches differ. For stateful chat you might see a difference, that's why we recommend staged canaries and consistency tests. We can automate a canary that warms the smaller model's prefix cache before cutover.
[06:28] Lena: Okay. What about multi-region routing for latency-sensitive traffic — prefer nearby region with fallback to other region if degraded?

[06:36] Maya: Yes, routing policies can be latency-first, cost-first, or hybrid. You can also set rules per-customer segment. For latency-first we pick the closest healthy region and only failover when health checks indicate degradation beyond thresholds.
[06:55] Ravi: Health checks — how frequent are they? Can we tune thresholds?
[06:59] Ethan: Health checks are configurable; default is per-10s active check plus passive failure detection from error rates. You can tune detection windows and sensitivity to avoid flapping.
[07:15] Nicole: Audit logs and observability — do we get token-level traces and per-model metrics?

[07:21] Maya: Yes, Redwood Console provides per-route and per-model dashboards, token-level cost and latency breakdowns, and tracing hooks. For Dedicated/Private we can retain logs for longer retention windows and integrate with your SIEM.
[07:35] Lena: Suppose a region has a hard outage and failover happens. What's typical RTO and user experience?

[07:44] Ethan: If you have active replication and warmed caches, RTO can be sub-30s. Without warmed caches, initial requests may take extra 200-800ms until caches warm. We recommend a staged policy: failover traffic to a smaller quantized model while cache warms to avoid big latency spikes.
[08:06] Tom: Does Redwood support graceful degradation — like returning partial answers or fallbacks to search?

[08:12] Ethan: We support configurable graceful degradation: cached responses, fallback to retrieval-augmented generation with local index, or degrade to short, predictive summaries. This is policy-driven and you can tie it to error budgets.
[08:29] Lena: For audits and incident response, can we see decision logs of routing/fallbacks?

[08:35] Maya: Yes, we provide routing decision logs and trace IDs for each request so you can reconstruct what happened during an incident. Those are part of the console and can be streamed to your logging bucket.
[08:49] Ravi: On the networking side, for Dedicated we want VPC peering and private links — is that supported?
[08:55] Ethan: Yes, Dedicated supports VPC peering, PrivateLink, and customer-managed networking. Private gives you full on-prem options.
[09:05] Tom: Cost question: if we run active replication and multi-region warm caches, how much does that add to per-token cost?
[09:12] Ethan: As I said earlier, rough ballpark is 10-25% for cache replication, plus inter-region egress. We'll model this for your expected traffic in the benchmark sheet.
[09:22] Lena: We also need to know what failure modes are common — like control-plane failures, network partition, or model runtime crashes — and how Redwood handles them.

[09:30] Ethan: Right. Common modes: node-level GPU OOM or stall, autoscaler delay under sudden bursts, network partition, or underlying cloud region outage. Our runtime uses request hedging, preemptive replica counts, and KV checkpointing to minimize impact. For Dedicated we can provision additional headroom to avoid autoscaler delays.

[09:54] Maya: We also have automatic fallback to model variants and duplicate routing to multiple regions (race and pick fastest) for really latency-sensitive paths; that's configurable but increases cost.
[10:07] Ravi: Race — you mean send the same request to two regions and take the first answer? That seems expensive.
[10:12] Ethan: Exactly, it's called hedging. It reduces tail latency but increases cost proportional to the hedged requests. Often used selectively for high-value transactions.
[10:25] Tom: For our compliance team, Nicole will send a list of 20-30 specific questions. How fast can Redwood respond?
[10:33] Maya: We can get the SOC2 pack and network diagram over within 48 hours and start answering compliance Qs in parallel. For bespoke items like HSM integration we'll have SE follow-up.
[10:43] Nicole: Great. On incident postmortem data, do you retain full request traces? For how long?

[10:50] Maya: Retention depends on plan — default retention on Hosted is 30 days; Dedicated/Enterprise can get longer retention windows. We can also stream logs to your storage for long-term retention.
[11:02] Lena: Let's talk about a hypothetical outage scenario: region A goes down for 10 minutes. Outline the sequence of events with default Hosted settings.

[11:10] Ethan: Default Hosted: passive error detection triggers after a threshold (60s-2m depending on error rate). Traffic will be retried and then routed to healthy region; if caches cold you'll see a latency bump. If model variant fallback is enabled, some traffic will hit a smaller model in the same region until failover completes. We'll include a decision flow in the runbook we send.
[11:35] Ravi: Is there a way to test failover in a controlled way?
[11:38] Ethan: Yes, we support chaos testing — you can run simulated region failovers in a staging environment and collect metrics. We also automate canary warm-ups and rollback if error rates spike.
[11:49] Tom: If we want guaranteed 99.99% availability for top-tier customers, what's the recommended deployment?
[11:56] Ethan: For 99.99% you'd almost certainly want Dedicated with multi-region active/passive plus warmed caches and hedging for tail latency. That usually requires reserved capacity commitment.
[12:07] Lena: How does Redwood handle rate limiting and throttling to prevent downstream overload during an incident?
[12:14] Ethan: We have hierarchical rate limits: global, customer, and route-level. In incidents we can prioritize routes and shed non-critical traffic automatically using policies you define.
[12:26] Nicole: Encryption keys — for Hosted BYOK, where are keys stored?
[12:30] Maya: BYOK uses your cloud KMS (e.g., AWS KMS, GCP KMS) tied to your account; keys can be region-scoped. For Dedicated/Private you can bring your HSM.
[12:41] Ravi: Can we do per-tenant routing rules to send EU users always to EU region unless fallback?
[12:46] Ethan: Yes, you can set routing rules by geo, customer segment, or even by request attributes. You can also set allowed fallback regions for compliance.
[12:57] Tom: About logs and auditing — can routing decisions be exported as JSON lines to our S3?
[13:03] Maya: Yes, decision logs and trace IDs can be exported; we'll provide examples in the security pack.
[13:12] Lena: Ok this is helpful. What about the mechanical details of canarying a new model across regions?

[13:19] Ethan: We support canary rollouts with traffic percentages, automated success criteria (latency, error rate, quality metrics). For multi-region canaries we can coordinate warm-ups so secondary regions prefetch prefixes.
[13:33] Ravi: Quality metrics — does Redwood integrate with eval harnesses for regression detection?
[13:38] Ethan: Yes, Redwood Optimize ties evals to rollouts. You can set prompt suites and get regression alerts; we can block rollouts that degrade quality beyond thresholds.
[13:50] Nicole: If we go Dedicated, is the network topology static or can we burst to hosted if demand spikes?
[13:56] Maya: Dedicated can be configured with burst-to-hosted fallback so if committed capacity is saturated, traffic can overflow to hosted variants, subject to policy and data handling rules.
[14:08] Tom: That could be useful. Any pitfalls with burst-to-hosted and data policies?
[14:13] Ethan: Make sure your data residency rules allow overflow. Also, your keys and audit controls differ when bursting to hosted; we recommend clear policies and allowed routes.
[14:24] Lena: For a pilot, what would you recommend we start with?

[14:28] Maya: Start with Hosted sandbox to validate feature quality and routing policies, then move to a Dedicated pilot with reserved capacity and a canary plan for failovers. Private if you need full HSM/on-prem control.
[14:38] Ravi: Timeline-wise, from pilot to production — what are realistic milestones?
[14:42] Ethan: Pilot could be 2-4 weeks depending on prompts and integration, Dedicated onboarding 4-8 weeks, Private can take longer depending on on-prem complexity.
[14:52] Tom: Cost modelling — can you send examples for our 2k qps profile with and without active replication?
[14:58] Maya: Yes, that's one of the items we'll include in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[15:05] Lena: Any references or customers doing exactly this?
[15:09] Maya: We have customers in fintech using Dedicated with multi-region failover and active replication for prefix caches — we'll include anonymized case studies.

[15:18] Tom: Let's capture explicit requirements from our side: 99.95% SLO, sub-500ms P90 for simple prompts, EU data residency for EU users, KMS BYOK, and ability to do canary failovers with pre-warm. We'll share docs.
[15:36] Maya: Noted. We'll send SOC2/ISO pack, routing runbook draft, and benchmark. Proposed SE deep dive next Wed — does that work?
[15:44] Lena: Works for us. Ravi will bring detailed traffic curves and Nicole will send compliance questions.
[15:51] Ethan: I'll draft the canary/fallback runbook and include diagrams for cache replication vs soft-fallback.
[16:00] Tom: Any other open concerns?
[16:03] Nicole: Latency spikes on cold failover are the main one; need mitigation strategies documented.
[16:09] Ethan: We'll add recommended mitigations: hedging for critical routes, warmed canaries, active replication for critical prefixes, and staged rollouts.
[16:18] Maya: Ok, recap of next steps: Maya to send security pack and benchmark; Ethan to send runbook; Ventura to send SLOs and compliance Qs. We'll schedule SE deep dive.
[16:30] Lena: Thanks all, we'll review and regroup after we see the materials.
[16:35] End of meeting
